stem:
Express the change in internal energy of a system when
(i) No heat is absorbed by the system from the surroundings, but work (w) is done on the system. What type of wall does the system have?
(ii) No work is done on the system, but \(q\) amount of heat is taken out from the system and given to the surroundings. What type of wall does the system have?
(iii) w amount of work is done by the system and \(q\) amount of heat is supplied to the system. What type of system would it be?
solution:
(i) \(\Delta U = \text{w}_{ad}\), wall is adiabatic.
(ii) \(\Delta U = -q\), thermally conducting walls.
(iii) \(\Delta U = q - \text{w}\), closed system.

stem: Two litres of an ideal gas at a pressure of \(10\,\text{atm}\) expands isothermally at \(25\,^\circ\text{C}\) into a vacuum until its total volume is 10 litres. How much heat is absorbed and how much work is done in the expansion?
solution:
We have \(q = -\text{w} = p_{ex}(10 - 2) = 0(8) = 0\).
No work is done; no heat is absorbed.

stem: Consider the same expansion, but this time against a constant external pressure of \(1\,\text{atm}\).
Consider the expansion given in problem 5.2, for 1 mol of an ideal gas conducted reversibly.
_note: The book prints the log argument as \(V_f/V_s\); the subscript should be \(i\) (initial volume), as the substitution 10/2 on the next line confirms. Transcribed as \(V_f/V_i\).

stem: If water vapour is assumed to be a perfect gas, molar enthalpy change for vapourisation of 1 mol of water at \(1\,\text{bar}\) and \(100\,^\circ\text{C}\) is \(41\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Calculate the internal energy change, when 1 mol of water is vapourised at \(1\,\text{bar}\) pressure and \(100\,^\circ\text{C}\).
solution:
(i) The change \(\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\)
\(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g\text{R}T\)
or \(\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g\text{R}T\); substituting the values, we get
\(\Delta U = 41.00\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1} - 1 \times 8.3\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} \times 373\,\text{K}\)
\(= 41.00\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1} - 3.096\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(= 37.904\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

subtopic: Measurement of ΔU and ΔH: Calorimetry
stem:
\(1\,\text{g}\) of graphite is burnt in a bomb calorimeter in excess of oxygen at \(298\,\text{K}\) and 1 atmospheric pressure according to the equation
\(\text{C (graphite)} + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(g)\)
During the reaction, temperature rises from \(298\,\text{K}\) to \(299\,\text{K}\). If the heat capacity of the bomb calorimeter is \(20.7\,\text{kJ/K}\), what is the enthalpy change for the above reaction at \(298\,\text{K}\) and \(1\,\text{atm}\)?
solution:
Suppose \(q\) is the quantity of heat from the reaction mixture and \(C_V\) is the heat capacity of the calorimeter, then the quantity of heat absorbed by the calorimeter
\(q = C_V \times \Delta T\)
Quantity of heat from the reaction will have the same magnitude but opposite sign because the heat lost by the system (reaction mixture) is equal to the heat gained by the calorimeter.
\(q = -C_V \times \Delta T = -20.7\,\text{kJ/K} \times (299 - 298)\,\text{K} = -20.7\,\text{kJ}\)
(Here, negative sign indicates the exothermic nature of the reaction.)
Thus, \(\Delta U\) for the combustion of the \(1\,\text{g}\) of graphite \(= -20.7\,\text{kJ}\)
For combustion of 1 mol of graphite,
\(= \dfrac{12.0\,\text{g mol}^{-1} \times (-20.7\,\text{kJ})}{1\,\text{g}} = -2.48 \times 10^{2}\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
Since \(\Delta n_g = 0\), \(\Delta H = \Delta U = -2.48 \times 10^{2}\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The book prints the unit of \(\Delta U\) for 1 g of graphite as \(\text{kJ K}^{-1}\); it is an energy, so the unit is \(\text{kJ}\) (and the next line, which divides by \(1\,\text{g}\) and multiplies by \(\text{g mol}^{-1}\), only yields \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) if it is \(\text{kJ}\)). Transcribed with the correct unit.

subtopic: Enthalpy Change, ΔrH of a Reaction – Reaction Enthalpy
stem:
A swimmer coming out from a pool is covered with a film of water weighing about \(18\,\text{g}\). How much heat must be supplied to evaporate this water at \(298\,\text{K}\)? Calculate the internal energy of vaporisation at \(298\,\text{K}\).
\(\Delta_{vap}H^{\ominus}\) for water at \(298\,\text{K} = 44.01\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
solution:
We can represent the process of evaporation as
\(\underset{1\,\text{mol}}{\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)} \xrightarrow{\;\text{vaporisation}\;} \underset{1\,\text{mol}}{\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)}\)
No. of moles in \(18\,\text{g}\) \(\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\) is \(= \dfrac{18\,\text{g}}{18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 1\,\text{mol}\)
Heat supplied to evaporate \(18\,\text{g}\) water at \(298\,\text{K}\)
\(= n \times \Delta_{vap}H^{\ominus} = (1\,\text{mol}) \times (44.01\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}) = 44.01\,\text{kJ}\)
(assuming steam behaving as an ideal gas).
\(\Delta_{vap}U = \Delta_{vap}H^{\ominus} - p\Delta V = \Delta_{vap}H^{\ominus} - \Delta n_g\text{R}T\)
\(\Delta_{vap}H^{\ominus} - \Delta n_g\text{R}T = 44.01\,\text{kJ} - (1)(8.314\,\text{JK}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1})(298\,\text{K})(10^{-3}\,\text{kJ J}^{-1})\)
\(\Delta_{vap}U^{\ominus} = 44.01\,\text{kJ} - 2.48\,\text{kJ} = 41.53\,\text{kJ}\)
_note: In the last two lines the book's standard-state superscript renders as a Latin \(V\) (\(\Delta_{vap}H^V\), \(\Delta_{vap}U^V\)); every other occurrence in the chapter sets it as the standard-state symbol \(\ominus\), so it is a typesetting fault and is transcribed as \(\ominus\).

subtopic: Enthalpy Change, ΔrH of a Reaction – Reaction Enthalpy
stem: Assuming the water vapour to be a perfect gas, calculate the internal energy change when 1 mol of water at \(100\,^\circ\text{C}\) and \(1\,\text{bar}\) pressure is converted to ice at \(0\,^\circ\text{C}\). Given the enthalpy of fusion of ice is \(6.00\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), heat capacity of water is \(4.2\,\text{J/g}\,^\circ\text{C}\).
solution:
The change takes place as follows:
Step 1: \(1\,\text{mol}\ \text{H}_2\text{O}(l,\,100\,^\circ\text{C}) \rightarrow 1\,\text{mol}\ \text{H}_2\text{O}(l,\,0\,^\circ\text{C})\); enthalpy change \(\Delta H_1\)
Step 2: \(1\,\text{mol}\ \text{H}_2\text{O}(l,\,0\,^\circ\text{C}) \rightarrow 1\,\text{mol}\ \text{H}_2\text{O}(s,\,0\,^\circ\text{C})\); enthalpy change \(\Delta H_2\)
Total enthalpy change will be
\(\Delta H = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2\)
\(\Delta H_1 = -(18 \times 4.2 \times 100)\,\text{J mol}^{-1} = -7560\,\text{J mol}^{-1} = -7.56\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta H_2 = -6.00\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
Therefore,
\(\Delta H = -7.56\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1} + (-6.00\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}) = -13.56\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
There is negligible change in the volume during the change from liquid to solid state.
Therefore, \(p\Delta V = \Delta n_g\text{R}T = 0\)
\(\Delta H = \Delta U = -13.56\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The stem as printed says the water is converted to ice; the book's own solution correctly treats the whole path as liquid cooling followed by freezing. Its Step 2 prints the product state as \(\text{H}_2\text{O}(S)\) with a capital S, transcribed as \(s\) (solid).
